newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France cheered by record 1996 trade surplus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France cheered by record 1996 trade surplus.

text.p: France announced a record 1996 trade surplus of 122 billion francs ($22 billion) on Tuesday, claimed the surge as more proof of economic upturn and competitiveness and predicted another fillip for the economy from exports this year.

The government also predicted the surplus could rise to 135-145 billion francs in 1997 and the dollar's rise versus the franc should lift the figure in the next year-and-a-half after the initial negative impact of pushing up import costs.

News of the surplus and the bullish 1997 outlook comes in the wake of other positive soundings for the economy, such as a survey showing markedly greater optimism among industrialists on the prospects for increased production, as well as a surprise drop in unemployment in December.

A key measure of economic performance comes on Wednesday with the release of data on consumer spending on manufactured products. Economists polled by Reuters predict a rise of 0.8 percent, helped in part by January discount sales.
"This trade surplus is a precursor to economic upturn," Yves Galland, junior minister for foreign trade, told a news conference, adding that the surplus was clearly "structural".

France's official forecast is for economic growth of 2.3 percent this year after an estimated 1.3 percent rise in 1996, but the government is already talking of growth exceeding its initial estimates for 1997.

Only about 20-25 percent of the 1996 trade surplus could be attributed to differences in the state of the world's competing economies, or about 20-30 billion francs, Galland said. Exports rose four percent in 1996 and imports 2.2 percent, he added.

Galland said a 15 percent climb in the value of the dollar against the franc since October had cut the surplus by 5-6 billion francs in 1996 because of the resulting rise in import and energy costs in the short term.

But once this wore off, and assuming a dollar level of about 5.70 francs to the dollar, the impact of cheaper French exports could boost the surplus in 1997 by about seven billion francs and lead to a surge of 25 billion francs in 1998, he said.
The franc is currently hovering around 5.66 per dollar.
Galland told reporters France's share of the world market in 1996 edged up to 5.6 percent from 5.5 percent in 1995 and this was second only to advances made by Italy and the United States.
One of France's main aims now was further emerging market penetration and mobilisation of small and medium-sized firms.

Hailing the success of their Italian counterparts, Galland predicted that 100,000 small and medium sized French companies which accounted for about six percent of exports could generate another 150 billion francs in exports and create 400,000 jobs.

Galland said France had registered its first trade surplus with Germany -- six billion francs, since the early 1970s. France ran up a deficit with Italy of 7.2 billion francs but said this was due largely to the short-term effect of a lira rise from undervalued levels, like with the dollar, but that the situation had improved in the second half of 1996.

France continued to run trade deficits with the United States and Japan, of 2.29 and 1.87 billion francs, respectively, representing a reduction of two percent from 1995 in the U.S. case and a cut of 12 percent in the deficit with Japan.

Although the trade data, and possibly the consumer spending figures on Wednesday, will compound the greater optimism being espoused by the centre-right government, the release of January unemployment data on Friday remains an unknown, menacing factor.
Despite falling by 29,000 in December, France's unemployment rate is still stuck at a record level of 12.7 percent.

Other data released on Friday is expected to show that Gross Domestic Product remained flat in the fourth quarter of last year. Consumer price data released on Tuesday showed inflation of 0.3 percent in January and the rate running at 1.8 percent year-on-year.
